strengths: The paper addresses a practical NLP question: how much labelled data makes specialised models competitive with general models. Comparing learning curves across four approaches, seven models, and eight datasets is more informative than comparing only extreme few-shot and full-data settings.

The substantial repetition—100 runs for encoder fine-tuning, generally 20 for other approaches, and 10 for ChatGPT—is valuable. Reporting performance spread alongside means exposes instability that single-run comparisons would miss.

The results support a useful conditional finding: fine-tuned encoders become competitive with relatively modest training sets on several topic and intent classification tasks, while some binary tasks require substantially more data.

The manuscript provides prompts, several training settings, and a source-code link. Its limitations explicitly acknowledge quantisation, restricted evaluation, model coverage, and dependence on a shared prompt.
weaknesses: The central annotation-budget claim needs complete label accounting. Section 3 creates a 20% validation split and uses early stopping without explaining whether validation labels are restricted alongside the reported training budget. Consequently, 10 or 100 training examples do not establish an equivalent total annotation requirement. Furthermore, two demonstrations per class require 28 examples for DB Pedia, which is incompatible with a ten-example pool unless an additional sampling rule or label source is used.

The variance-aware break-even criterion is insufficiently specified and statistically overinterpreted. Figure 1 suggests non-overlap of mean-plus/minus-standard-deviation bands, but this does not establish a worst-case guarantee or a calibrated probability of outperforming another model. The crossing algorithm, interpolation between tested sizes, and aggregation underlying the claimed average 100–200% increase are unspecified. A reproducible definition and uncertainty estimates for performance differences and crossing locations are needed.

The prompting baselines need stronger validation because their quality directly determines the break-even thresholds. All models share one prompt developed on Mistral, with a fixed two demonstrations per class and no sensitivity analysis. Table 1 also describes BoolQ as determining whether a passage contains an answer, which differs from answering its yes/no question. Correct task wording and targeted checks across reasonable prompts and demonstration counts are necessary before making broad recommendations.

Several conclusions exceed the reported results. The explicit claim that at most 100 examples suffice on multiclass datasets to outperform any compared model conflicts with Table 2: RoBERTa versus Flan-T5 in-context learning on AG News requires 350 examples for the mean crossing and 1,100 when accounting for spread. Binary tasks also contain multi-thousand-example thresholds and missing crossings. The headline and recommendations should communicate these conditions and exceptions.

Evaluation and reproduction details remain incomplete. The limitations disclose 1,000-example test subsets for larger models and ChatGPT evaluation only at the 1,000-example training-pool setting, qualifying the main experimental description. It is unclear whether methods use identical evaluation examples; unequal test sampling would affect the variance used to determine crossings. Exact checkpoint identifiers, LoRA settings, truncation rules, and generated-output-to-label mapping also need documentation.

The broader interpretations require qualification. Binary versus multiclass comparisons also vary task type and difficulty, so class count is not isolated as an explanation. Prior benchmark exposure in instruction-tuned models is not examined, limiting interpretation of ten-example adaptation as learning a new task. Recommendations about resource-optimal methods and generation tasks are not supported by corresponding cost measurements or experiments. The label-budget and break-even-analysis concerns are decisive for OA 2: they require clarification and targeted validation before a positive Findings recommendation.
